fig.caption: The Sun drives the water cycle: evaporation, condensation, rain and infiltration into the ground.
fig.alt: Water cycle diagram

check.q: Droplets form on the outside of a glass of ice water. This is:
check.why: Water vapour in the air cools on touching the cold glass and condenses into droplets.

sections.md:
When rain soaks into the soil (**infiltration**), it trickles down through gaps between soil particles and rocks until it reaches a layer it cannot pass. The water collects there and fills the spaces. This is **groundwater**. The upper surface of this water-filled zone is the **water table**. Layers of rock and soil that hold usable groundwater are called **aquifers**.

We draw groundwater through wells, hand pumps and borewells. In many parts of India, most drinking water and irrigation water comes from the ground.

**Why is the water table falling in many places?**
- Too many borewells pumping more water than rain can replace.
- Concrete roads and buildings stop rain from seeping in.
- Cutting forests reduces infiltration; water runs off instead.
- Less rain in some years.

**Keeping the balance:**
- **Rainwater harvesting:** collecting rooftop rainwater into tanks or guiding it into recharge pits.
- Traditional systems: stepwells (baolis) in Rajasthan and Gujarat, johads, tankas, and the bamboo drip irrigation of Meghalaya.
- Drip irrigation and careful water use at home: closing taps, fixing leaks.

> Did you know? Chennai made rooftop rainwater harvesting compulsory for buildings in the early 2000s, and many areas saw groundwater levels improve.

check.q: Which action helps raise the water table?
check.why: Recharge pits let rainwater seep into the ground, refilling the groundwater.

sections.md:
| Mode | Needs a medium? | Where it happens | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Conduction | Yes, mainly solids | Particles pass energy along | Hot spoon handle |
| Convection | Yes, liquids and gases | Particles move and carry heat | Boiling water, sea breeze |
| Radiation | No | Through space and air | Sunlight, bonfire warmth |

Often all three happen at once. In a kitchen: the flame **radiates** to your hands, the pan bottom **conducts** heat to the food, and the oil or water inside circulates by **convection**. In nature, the Sun's radiation warms land and sea unequally, which drives winds by convection, which carry evaporated water into clouds — the water cycle — which refills rivers and groundwater.

**Did you know?** Desert animals like the fennec fox have huge ears full of blood vessels that help them radiate away extra body heat.

check.q: Which mode of heat transfer can work through a vacuum?
check.why: Radiation needs no medium, which is how the Sun's heat crosses space.

story.title: Grandmother's Matka and the Dry Well

parts.md: In a village near Jodhpur, Tara's grandmother kept a clay matka in the shade of the verandah. In the blazing May afternoon, its water was cool and sweet. 'How does it stay cold without a fridge?' Tara asked. Grandmother wiped the damp outside of the pot. 'The pot sweats, and the sweat flies away into the air, taking the heat with it.' Tara later learnt the word: evaporation.

That year the village well ran dry before the monsoon. An engineer came and explained that too many borewells were pulling water out faster than the rain could put it back. The villagers dug recharge pits and restored an old johad. When the rains came, the water soaked in instead of rushing away. Next summer the well had water again. Tara drew the whole water cycle on the school wall, with a matka in one corner and a well in the other.

workedExamples.q: Ravi says, 'Cold flows from the ice into my hand.' Is he right?
steps: Heat always flows from hotter to colder objects.
The hand is hotter than ice.
So heat flows from the hand into the ice, making the hand feel cold.
workedExamples.answer: No — heat flows from his hand to the ice.

workedExamples.q: Why are ventilators placed near the ceiling of a room?
steps: Breathing and lamps warm the air.
Warm air is lighter and rises.
Ventilators at the top let warm air escape so fresh, cool air can enter below.
workedExamples.answer: Because warm air rises by convection and escapes from the top.

workedExamples.q: Two identical tumblers of water, one wrapped in black paper and one in white, are kept in the sun. Which warms faster and why?
workedExamples.answer: The black one, because it absorbs more of the Sun's radiation.

workedExamples.q: Why does a borewell in a city go dry even after a normal monsoon?
steps: Concrete and roads stop rain from infiltrating
Many borewells pump out more than is recharged
So the water table falls below the borewell
workedExamples.answer: Less infiltration and over-pumping lower the water table.

summary: Heat flows from a hotter body to a colder body until temperatures become equal.
Temperature is measured in °C with a thermometer.
Conduction: heat moves through solids from particle to particle; metals conduct well.
Wood, plastic, air and cloth are insulators.
Convection: heated liquids and gases rise, cooler ones sink, forming currents.
Sea breeze by day, land breeze by night — both convection; monsoons are a giant version.
Radiation needs no medium; the Sun's heat reaches us this way.
Dark surfaces absorb more heat; light surfaces reflect more.
Woollens and blankets work by trapping air; a thermos reduces all three modes.
The Sun drives the water cycle: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection, infiltration.
Water that seeps into the ground forms groundwater; its top is the water table; aquifers store it.
Over-pumping and concrete lower the water table; rainwater harvesting and traditional systems help recharge it.

glossary.d: A loop of moving fluid carrying heat.
Heat transfer without a medium.
Cool wind from sea to land during the day.
Seeping of water into the ground.
Upper level of groundwater below the surface.
Rock or soil layer that holds usable groundwater.

practice: Name the three modes of heat transfer and give one example of each.
Why do cooking pans have copper bottoms?
Explain, with a diagram, how a sea breeze forms.
Why is it cooler near the sea in the afternoon?
Why do we feel warmer in dark clothes on a sunny winter day?
How does a woollen sweater keep us warm?
How does heat from the Sun reach the Earth?
Draw and label the water cycle.
What is the water table? Give two reasons why it is falling in many places.
Describe two ways of rainwater harvesting.
Why are two thin blankets warmer than one thick blanket?

rd-school-c7-new-science.light.title: Light: Shadows and Reflections
rd-school-c7-new-science.light.subtitle: Straight lines, dark shapes and mirror tricks

sections.h: A puppet show in the dark
sections.md:
Diwali night. The lights go out and someone switches on a torch. Your little sister makes a barking dog shadow on the wall with her hands. Your grandfather says Andhra Pradesh's *tholu bommalata* and Odisha's *ravana chhaya* leather puppet shows used exactly this trick centuries ago.

Why does a shadow form? Why does it have the same outline as your hand but no colours? And why does a mirror show your right hand as your left? To answer, we must learn how light behaves.

**Sources of light.** Objects that give out their own light are **luminous**: the Sun, stars, a candle flame, a bulb, a firefly, a glow-worm. Objects that do not, like the Moon, a book or your face, are **non-luminous**. We see them only because light from a source bounces off them into our eyes. The Moon shines only because it reflects sunlight.

**How do we see?** Light from a source falls on an object, bounces off it, and enters our eyes. In a completely dark room you see nothing, not because your eyes stop working, but because no light reaches them.

check.q: Which of these is a luminous object?
check.why: A firefly produces its own light; the Moon and mirrors only reflect light from other sources.

sections.md:
Hold different things in front of a torch:

- **Transparent** — light passes almost completely; you can see clearly through them: clear glass, clean water, air, clear plastic.
- **Translucent** — light passes partly; you see blurry shapes: butter paper, frosted glass, a thin cotton cloth, oily paper, tissue paper.
- **Opaque** — no light passes: wood, metal, stone, cardboard, your hand.

**Activity:** look at a lit bulb through each material and record whether you see it clearly, hazily or not at all. Then rub a drop of oil on a piece of plain paper and look again: the oily patch turns from opaque to translucent!

Only opaque (and to some extent translucent) objects make clear shadows.

head: Object
Type
Can you see through it?
fig.caption: Sorting materials by how they let light through.

check.q: Butter paper is:
check.why: Butter paper lets some light through, so we see only blurred shapes through it.

sections.md:
Take three cardboard sheets, punch a hole in the middle of each, and line them up in front of a candle. You can see the flame only when the three holes are in a perfectly straight line — check by passing a thread through all three holes and pulling it tight. Shift one sheet slightly and the flame disappears.

Try looking at a candle through a straight pipe, then through a bent one — you see it only through the straight one. This shows that **light travels in straight lines**. This property is called the **rectilinear propagation of light**. A narrow stream of light is a **ray**; many rays together form a **beam**. In diagrams a ray is drawn as a straight line with an arrow showing its direction.

Sunbeams streaming through a gap in the curtains, the beam of a lighthouse, laser pointers at a cricket stadium — all are straight. You see the beam itself only when dust or mist in the air scatters some light towards you.

check.q: Why can you not see a candle through a bent pipe?
check.why: Light cannot bend around the curve of the pipe because it travels in straight lines.

sections.md:
Because light travels straight, an opaque object blocks some rays, leaving a dark region behind it — a **shadow**. To get a shadow we need three things: a **source of light**, an **opaque object**, and a **screen** (wall, ground) to fall on.

Facts about shadows:
- A shadow is always dark (black or grey) whatever the colour of the object. A red ball and a blue ball give the same dark shadow.
- A shadow shows the outline, not details.
- The size changes: move the object closer to the torch and the shadow grows; move it closer to the screen and it shrinks.
- The same object can make different shadows. A pencil can cast a long rectangle or a small circle depending on how it is held; a cone can cast a triangle or a circle.
- Translucent objects cast faint, light shadows; transparent ones hardly any.

Shadows also tell time. Your shadow is longest in the morning and evening (Sun low in the sky) and shortest at noon (Sun high overhead). A **sundial**, like the giant Samrat Yantra at Jantar Mantar in Jaipur, uses a shadow to tell the time.

**Eclipses** are giant shadows: in a solar eclipse the Moon's shadow falls on Earth; in a lunar eclipse Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.

check.q: A green leaf held in sunlight casts a shadow. Its colour is:
check.why: A shadow is simply a region where light is blocked, so it is always dark regardless of the object's colour.

sections.md:
You can build a camera with no lens. Take a box (or two tubes that slide into each other), make a tiny pinhole on one side and fix tracing paper on the opposite side. Point the pinhole at a bright scene — a lit bulb or a building in sunlight — with a dark cloth over your head to keep out stray light.

You'll see a small **upside-down** (inverted) image on the paper, with left and right swapped too. Rays from the top of the object travel in straight lines through the pinhole and land at the bottom of the screen, and rays from the bottom land at the top.

**Experiments:** slide the screen farther from the pinhole and the image grows but becomes dimmer. Make the hole bigger and the image becomes brighter but blurred.

**Never look at the Sun directly**, even through a pinhole camera's tube; view only the image on the screen.

Nature makes pinhole cameras too. Under a leafy tree at noon, the round spots of light on the ground are images of the Sun made by tiny gaps between leaves. During a partial solar eclipse these spots become crescents!

check.q: The image in a pinhole camera is:
check.why: Rays cross at the pinhole in straight lines, so the top of the object appears at the bottom of the image.

sections.md:
When light falls on a shiny smooth surface it bounces back. This is **reflection**. A **mirror** is a very smooth, polished surface — usually glass with a thin silvery (or aluminium) coating behind it.

Shine a torch through a comb (or a slit in black paper) onto a mirror standing on a sheet of paper. You see a ray striking the mirror and bouncing off.
- The ray that hits the mirror is the **incident ray**.
- The ray that bounces off is the **reflected ray**.
- An imaginary line drawn at 90° to the mirror where the ray hits is the **normal**.

Measure the angles with a protractor: the angle between the incident ray and the normal (**angle of incidence**) equals the angle between the reflected ray and the normal (**angle of reflection**). Tilt the torch and both change together. This is the **law of reflection**.

**Regular and diffused reflection.** A mirror or still water reflects parallel rays in one direction — **regular reflection** — so you see a clear image. A rough surface like paper, a wall or cloth scatters rays in many directions — **diffused (irregular) reflection** — so you see the object but no image. Diffused reflection is what lets us see most things around us.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#f4f8fb'/><rect x='80' y='240' width='440' height='10' fill='#8fb3cc'/><text x='300' y='275' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='14'>plane mirror</text><line x1='300' y1='240' x2='300' y2='60' stroke='#888' stroke-dasharray='5 5'/><text x='305' y='55' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='13'>normal</text><line x1='120' y1='70' x2='300' y2='240' stroke='#f0a400' stroke-width='4' stroke-dasharray='260' stroke-dashoffset='260'><animate attributeName='stroke-dashoffset' values='260;0;0' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></line><line x1='300' y1='240' x2='480' y2='70' stroke='#e2554f' stroke-width='4' stroke-dasharray='260' stroke-dashoffset='260'><animate attributeName='stroke-dashoffset' values='260;260;0' keyTimes='0;0.5;1' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></line><text x='130' y='60' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='14'>incident ray</text><text x='420' y='60' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='14'>reflected ray</text><text x='240' y='200' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='13'>i</text><text x='352' y='200' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='13'>r</text><text x='300' y='120' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='13' fill='#555'>angle i = angle r</text></svg>

fig.alt: Animated reflection of a ray

check.q: A ray strikes a mirror at an angle of incidence of 35°. The angle of reflection is:
check.why: By the law of reflection, the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, 35°.

sections.md:
**Image in a plane mirror:**
- It is **erect** (right side up).
- It is the **same size** as the object.
- It appears as far **behind** the mirror as the object is in front.
- It is **laterally inverted** — left and right are swapped. Raise your right hand and your mirror twin raises its left. That's why AMBULANCE is painted in mirror writing on the front of ambulances, so drivers read it correctly in their rear-view mirror.
- It cannot be caught on a screen placed behind the mirror; it only *appears* to be there.

Letters such as A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y look the same in a mirror, because they have a vertical line of symmetry.

Even still lake water and polished steel plates reflect, but rough surfaces scatter light in all directions.

check.q: Why is 'AMBULANCE' written in mirror letters on the vehicle?
options: So it reads correctly in a driver's mirror due to lateral inversion
check.why: A plane mirror swaps left and right, so mirror writing appears normal when seen in a rear-view mirror.

sections.md:
Look at your face in a shiny steel spoon. On the inner, caved-in side your face may look large when the spoon is close, and upside down when it is farther away. On the outer, bulging side your face always looks small and upright.

These are **spherical mirrors** — parts of a hollow sphere:
- **Concave mirror** — reflecting surface curves inward (like the inside of the spoon). It can form enlarged, erect images when the object is very close, and inverted images when the object is farther away. It can also gather sunlight to a bright spot.
- **Convex mirror** — reflecting surface bulges outward (like the back of the spoon). It always forms small, erect images, but shows a much wider area.

| Mirror | Uses |
|---|---|
| Plane | dressing mirrors, periscopes, kaleidoscopes |
| Concave | shaving and make-up mirrors, dentists' mirrors, torch and car headlight reflectors, solar cookers |
| Convex | rear-view (side) mirrors of vehicles, mirrors at sharp hill road bends, shop security mirrors |

The rear-view mirror of a scooter is convex because the driver needs to see a wide stretch of road behind.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 260' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><path d='M140 40 Q90 130 140 220' fill='none' stroke='#2563eb' stroke-width='6'/><g stroke='#f59e0b' stroke-width='2'><line x1='20' y1='80' x2='118' y2='80'/><line x1='20' y1='130' x2='108' y2='130'/><line x1='20' y1='180' x2='118' y2='180'/><line x1='118' y1='80' x2='60' y2='130'><animate attributeName='opacity' values='0.3;1;0.3' dur='2s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></line><line x1='118' y1='180' x2='60' y2='130'><animate attributeName='opacity' values='0.3;1;0.3' dur='2s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></line></g><path d='M440 40 Q490 130 440 220' fill='none' stroke='#16a34a' stroke-width='6'/><g stroke='#f59e0b' stroke-width='2'><line x1='330' y1='80' x2='462' y2='80'/><line x1='330' y1='180' x2='462' y2='180'/><line x1='462' y1='80' x2='380' y2='30'/><line x1='462' y1='180' x2='380' y2='230'/></g><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='14'><text x='60' y='245'>concave: gathers light</text><text x='360' y='252'>convex: spreads light, wide view</text></g></svg>
fig.caption: A concave mirror brings parallel rays together; a convex mirror spreads them out.
fig.alt: Concave and convex mirror ray diagrams

check.q: Which mirror is used as a rear-view mirror in vehicles?
check.why: A convex mirror gives an erect, smaller image of a much wider area, so the driver sees more of the road behind.

sections.md:
With two plane mirrors tilted at 45° at the two ends of a tube, you can see over a wall — a **periscope**. Light from the object hits the top mirror, reflects down the tube, hits the bottom mirror and reflects into your eye. Submarines and soldiers in bunkers use this idea.

Two or three mirrors placed at an angle make many images — the principle of a **kaleidoscope**, where coloured bangle pieces create endless symmetric patterns. Two mirrors at 60° show 5 images of an object (6 copies including the object), arranged in a lovely pattern; at 90°, 3 images.

Mirrors in a barber shop facing each other give an 'infinite corridor' of images because the light keeps bouncing back and forth.

**Did you know?** Light travels about 3 lakh kilometres every second. It takes only about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach us from the Sun.

check.q: In a periscope, the mirrors are placed at what angle to the tube?
check.why: At 45°, each mirror turns the light through a right angle, sending it down the tube and then into the eye.

story.title: The Mirror on the Mountain Road

parts.md: Anil was travelling by bus from Dehradun to Mussoorie with his class. The road twisted like a ribbon. At one sharp bend, the driver slowed and glanced at a big round orange-framed mirror on a pole. In it, Anil saw a tiny truck coming round the corner — a truck he could not see directly because of the hill. 'Why is everything so small in that mirror?' he asked his teacher.

At the hotel, Ms. Rao handed him a steel spoon. 'Look at the back.' Anil saw his face tiny but right side up, with the whole room behind him. 'That's a convex mirror,' she said. 'Small images, but a wide view — so the driver sees the whole bend.' Anil turned the spoon round and his face jumped upside down. He spent the rest of the evening testing every shiny thing in the hotel, and wrote in his diary: 'A bent mirror is a mirror that sees more.'

workedExamples.q: You stand 2 m in front of a plane mirror. How far is your image from you?
steps: The image is as far behind the mirror as you are in front: 2 m.
Distance from you to image = 2 m + 2 m.

workedExamples.q: If you walk 1 m closer to that mirror, how far is the image from you now?
steps: You are now 1 m from the mirror.

workedExamples.q: A ray makes an angle of 60° with the mirror surface. Find the angle of reflection.
steps: Angle of reflection = angle of incidence

workedExamples.q: How would the word 'TOM' look in a mirror, and why?
steps: T, O and M are symmetric about a vertical line, so each letter looks the same
But the order is reversed by lateral inversion

summary: Luminous objects give their own light; non-luminous objects reflect it.
We see objects when light from them enters our eyes.
Materials are transparent, translucent or opaque.
Light travels in straight lines (rectilinear propagation).
A shadow forms when an opaque object blocks light; it needs a source, object and screen.
Shadows are dark regardless of object colour; their size changes with distances.
A pinhole camera gives an inverted image.
Reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection, measured from the normal.
Smooth surfaces give regular reflection; rough surfaces give diffused reflection.
A plane mirror image is erect, same size, as far behind as the object is in front, and laterally inverted.
Concave mirrors can enlarge and gather light; convex mirrors give small, erect images with a wide view.
Periscopes and kaleidoscopes use plane mirrors.

rd-school-c7-science-a.ch01-nutrition-in.title: Nutrition in Plants
rd-school-c7-science-a.ch01-nutrition-in.subtitle: How a leaf cooks food from sunlight, air and water

sections.md:
Your mother cooks rice, dal and sabzi. A goat eats grass. A tiger eats the goat. But who feeds the grass? A mango tree in your school grows from a seed to a giant weighing many tonnes — and nobody ever serves it lunch. Where does all that mass come from?

The answer is one of the most important processes on Earth. Plants make their own food. In this read we'll see how, and also meet some strange plants that eat insects, steal food, live on dead matter or share food with partners — and finally how the soil gets back what plants take from it.

**Nutrients** are the components of food that our bodies need: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins and minerals. **Nutrition** is the way an organism takes in food and uses it. All living things need food for energy to do work, for growth, for repair of damaged parts and for staying healthy.

check.q: Which of these is NOT a reason organisms need food?
check.why: Food gives energy, helps growth and repairs the body; turning sunlight into soil is not something food does.

sections.h: Modes of nutrition: autotrophs and heterotrophs
sections.md:
There are two main modes of nutrition:

- **Autotrophic nutrition** (*auto* = self, *trophos* = nourishment): the organism makes its own food from simple substances. Green plants are **autotrophs**.
- **Heterotrophic nutrition** (*heteros* = other): the organism depends on others for food — directly on plants, or on animals that ate plants. Animals, humans and most fungi are **heterotrophs**.

Every food chain begins with an autotroph. When you eat a paneer roll, the paneer came from a cow that ate grass. Ultimately, all our food can be traced back to plants. And the energy in all that food came first from the **Sun** — the Sun is the ultimate source of energy for nearly all living things.

right.title: Heterotrophs
points: Eat plants or animals or dead matter

check.q: Which of these is an autotroph?
check.why: A neem tree is a green plant that makes its own food by photosynthesis.

sections.md:
Before we enter the leaf factory, a quick look at what bodies are made of. All living things are built of tiny units called **cells**, visible only under a microscope. Some organisms, such as amoeba, are a single cell. Others, like you and a banyan tree, are made of crores of cells.

A cell is enclosed by a thin outer boundary, the **cell membrane**. Inside it is a jelly-like **cytoplasm**, and usually a central **nucleus** that controls the cell's activities. Plant cells also have a stiff **cell wall** outside the membrane, and the cells of green parts of plants have tiny green bodies called **chloroplasts** — the actual kitchens where food is made. Look at a thin onion peel under a school microscope and you can see the brick-like cells with their walls.

check.q: Which part of a plant cell contains chlorophyll?
check.why: Chlorophyll is found in chloroplasts, where photosynthesis takes place.

sections.md:
Leaves are the **food factories** of a plant. They contain a green pigment, **chlorophyll**, inside chloroplasts. Chlorophyll traps the energy of sunlight. Using that energy, the leaf combines **carbon dioxide** (from air) and **water** (from soil) to make **carbohydrates** (glucose, later stored as starch). Oxygen is released.

**Carbon dioxide + Water → (sunlight, chlorophyll) → Carbohydrate + Oxygen**

How do the raw materials arrive?
- **Water and minerals** are absorbed by roots from the soil and carried up through vessel-like tubes in the stem to the leaves — like pipes supplying water to the top of a building.
- **Carbon dioxide** enters through tiny pores on the leaf surface called **stomata** (singular: stoma). Each stoma is surrounded by two **guard cells** that open and close it. Oxygen and water vapour leave through the same pores.

The word *photosynthesis* means 'putting together with light'. Without sunlight there is no photosynthesis — which is why plants kept in a dark cupboard turn pale and weak.

**From sugar to everything else.** The glucose made in leaves is used for energy and also converted into other substances: it is stored as **starch**, and the plant also makes **fats** and **proteins** from carbohydrates (proteins need nitrogen from the soil too).

**Did you know?** Photosynthesis also supplies nearly all the oxygen in the air we breathe. Life on Earth would be almost impossible without it.

keyTerms: Chlorophyll — green pigment that traps sunlight
Stomata — tiny pores on leaves for gas exchange
Guard cells — open and close the stomata
Photosynthesis — making food using light

check.q: Through which part does carbon dioxide enter a leaf?
check.why: Stomata are tiny pores on leaves through which gases like carbon dioxide enter and oxygen leaves.

sections.md:
**Green stems and branches** also contain chlorophyll and make some food.

**Desert plants** such as cactus have leaves reduced to **spines** to cut water loss. Their thick green **stems** carry out photosynthesis instead.

**Leaves that are not green.** Red, brown or purple leaves (like those of some crotons or red amaranth) also contain chlorophyll; its green colour is just hidden by large amounts of other pigments.

**Algae.** The slimy green patches in ponds and stagnant water are **algae**. They contain chlorophyll and make their own food.

**Variegated leaves** (green with white patches, as in some money plants) make starch only in the green parts — a neat way to show chlorophyll is needed.

> Did you know? The cells of a leaf containing chlorophyll also need a constant supply of water; on a hot afternoon, a plant may lose so much water through its stomata that the guard cells close them, slowing photosynthesis.

check.q: In a cactus, photosynthesis mainly happens in the:
check.why: Cactus leaves are reduced to spines, so the thick green stem carries out photosynthesis.

sections.md:
Glucose made in leaves is stored as **starch**. Starch turns **blue-black** with iodine solution — a simple test you can do in school.

**Activity: is sunlight needed?**
1. Keep a potted plant in the dark for two days so its leaves use up their starch.
2. Cover part of one leaf with black paper on both sides and put the plant in sunlight for a few hours.
3. Pluck the leaf, boil it in water, then in alcohol in a water bath (under a teacher's supervision) to remove chlorophyll.
4. Rinse and add a few drops of dilute iodine solution.

The part that received sunlight turns blue-black; the covered part does not. This proves that **sunlight is needed for photosynthesis**.

**Variations:** test a variegated leaf — only the parts that were green turn blue-black (chlorophyll is needed). Keep a plant in a sealed jar with a substance that absorbs carbon dioxide — its leaves show no starch (CO₂ is needed).

check.q: Starch gives which colour with iodine?
check.why: Iodine reacts with starch to give a blue-black colour, proving that food was made in that part of the leaf.

sections.md:
Carbohydrates contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. But plants also make **proteins**, which need **nitrogen**. Air is about 78% nitrogen, yet plants cannot absorb it directly from the air.

Help comes from **bacteria** in the soil. Some of these bacteria convert atmospheric nitrogen into soluble forms that roots can absorb along with water. A special group, **Rhizobium**, lives in the root nodules of **leguminous plants** — gram, peas, moong, beans, groundnut. Rhizobium gives the plant usable nitrogen; the plant gives Rhizobium food and shelter. This partnership is an example of **symbiosis**.

That is why farmers often grow pulses between cereal crops: the legumes naturally enrich soil with nitrogen, so less fertiliser is needed for the next crop.

check.q: Rhizobium bacteria live in the roots of:
check.why: Rhizobium forms root nodules in leguminous plants like gram and peas and fixes nitrogen for them.

sections.h: Other modes of nutrition in plants
sections.md:
Not all plants are fully autotrophic.

**Parasites.** *Cuscuta* (amarbel) is a yellow, wiry, leafless plant that winds around host plants like ber or jasmine. It has no chlorophyll. It sends special roots (haustoria) into the host and sucks its food. The host loses valuable nutrients. An organism that lives on and feeds from another is a **parasite**; the one it feeds from is the **host**. (Animals like mosquitoes and lice that feed on us are parasites too.)

**Insectivorous plants.** The **pitcher plant** (found in the hills of Meghalaya) has a leaf shaped like a jug, with the leaf tip forming a lid. Insects attracted to it slip inside, get trapped by downward-pointing hairs and are digested by juices. The **Venus flytrap** and **sundew** also trap insects. These plants are green and photosynthesise, but they grow in nitrogen-poor soil and get extra nitrogen from insects.

**Symbiosis.** Some organisms live together and share food and shelter. In a **lichen**, a fungus and an alga live as partners: the alga has chlorophyll and makes food; the fungus provides shelter, water and minerals. Some fungi also live in tree roots, helping them absorb nutrients while receiving food.

head: Type
Example
How it gets food
fig.caption: Modes of nutrition among plants and fungi.

check.q: Cuscuta is a:
check.why: Cuscuta has no chlorophyll and takes ready-made food from its host plant, so it is a parasite.

sections.md:
You may have seen fluffy patches on old bread, or umbrella-shaped mushrooms on rotting logs in the rains. These are **fungi**. They have no chlorophyll, so they cannot make food.

**Activity: grow bread mould.** Moisten a piece of bread and keep it in a warm, dark, humid place for 2–3 days. White-grey cotton-like threads appear, later with black dots. Under a magnifier you can see the threads clearly. (Do not smell or eat it; wash hands afterwards.)

Fungi release **digestive juices** onto dead and decaying matter, turn it into a solution, and absorb the nutrients. This mode is called **saprotrophic nutrition**, and the organisms are **saprotrophs**.

Fungal **spores** float in the air everywhere. When they land on something moist and warm, they grow. That's why bread, pickles, leather and clothes spoil in humid monsoon weather. Keep food dry and covered.

Some fungi are useful: yeast in idli batter and bread, mushrooms we eat, and the fungi that make medicines like penicillin. Some mushrooms are poisonous, so never eat wild ones.

check.q: Why does bread spoil quickly in the rainy season?
options: Fungal spores grow fast in warm, humid conditions
check.why: Moisture and warmth help fungal spores from the air germinate and grow on the bread.

sections.h: How nutrients are replenished in the soil
sections.md:
Every crop takes minerals out of the soil. Over seasons, the soil would become poor if nothing returned them. Farmers add **manure** (decomposed plant and animal waste) and **fertilisers** containing nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Crop rotation with legumes, as we saw, adds nitrogen naturally.

In forests and gardens, fallen leaves, dead plants and animals are broken down by saprotrophic fungi and bacteria, returning minerals to the soil. Nature runs its own recycling system.

**Did you know?** A single large tree can release enough oxygen in a year for a few people — one more reason to plant and protect trees.

check.q: Which practice naturally adds nitrogen to soil?
check.why: Legumes host Rhizobium, which fixes atmospheric nitrogen into the soil.

parts.md: In a village near Nashik stood an old banyan, Grandma Banyan, older than anyone could remember. One morning a squirrel asked her, 'Grandma, I see you never eat. How are you so big?' The banyan rustled. 'My lunchbox is the sky. Every leaf is a little kitchen. The Sun is my fire, the air gives me carbon dioxide, and my roots sip water from deep below. I mix them in my green chloroplasts and out comes sweet sugar — and a gift of oxygen for you.'

A mushroom near her roots chuckled, 'I can't cook. I eat the fallen leaves you drop.' A yellow Cuscuta vine clinging to a nearby bush blushed. 'And I... borrow from my host.' A gram plant in the next field waved its roots: 'I have tiny friends, Rhizobium, who bring me nitrogen.' The banyan smiled. 'Everyone has a way to eat. But remember — all your food began in a green leaf.' The squirrel looked at the jamun in its paws and understood.

workedExamples.q: A plant is kept in a dark room for a week. Predict what happens and why.
steps: The plant uses up stored food.
It cannot make more, so it becomes weak, pale and may die.
workedExamples.answer: It weakens because photosynthesis needs light.

workedExamples.q: Why do farmers grow gram after a wheat crop?
steps: Gram is a legume with Rhizobium in its root nodules.
Rhizobium fixes atmospheric nitrogen, enriching the soil.

workedExamples.q: A variegated leaf (green with white patches) is tested with iodine after being in sunlight. What do you expect?
workedExamples.answer: Only the green parts turn blue-black, showing chlorophyll is needed.

workedExamples.q: Why is the pitcher plant called insectivorous even though it is green?
steps: It photosynthesises like other green plants
It traps and digests insects to get extra nitrogen
workedExamples.answer: It eats insects to make up for missing nitrogen, while still making its own carbohydrates.

summary: Nutrition is how organisms obtain and use food for energy, growth and repair.
Green plants are autotrophs; animals and fungi are heterotrophs; the Sun is the ultimate energy source.
All living things are made of cells; plant cells have a cell wall and chloroplasts.
Photosynthesis: CO₂ + water → (sunlight, chlorophyll) → carbohydrate + oxygen.
Leaves are the food factories; stomata let gases in and out; guard cells control stomata.
Water and minerals come from roots through the stem.
Green stems (cactus), coloured leaves and algae also photosynthesise.
Starch turns blue-black with iodine; the test shows light and chlorophyll are needed.
Plants make fats and proteins too; proteins need nitrogen.
Rhizobium in legume root nodules fixes nitrogen (symbiosis).
Cuscuta is a parasite; pitcher plant is insectivorous.
Fungi are saprotrophs that feed on dead matter; spores grow in warm, humid conditions.
Lichens show symbiosis between fungus and alga.
Manure, fertilisers and legumes replenish soil nutrients.

glossary.d: Organism that makes its own food.
Green body in plant cells where photosynthesis occurs.
Organism feeding on dead and decaying matter.
Close relationship in which two organisms help each other.
Organism from which a parasite takes food.
